text:
Moth and Gravel, Field Note 8. A
whole staircase, one undo, an AI

narrated edition of the
published note. The thing you

just tried, you meant to build a
little way across the island,

three pieces perhaps, a run of
ramps, something the pony could

try. You place it, look again,
and change your mind. How many

times should you have to undo?
The machine can count the

pieces. The player has a
different unit, the thing they

just tried. That is the small
design question inside Sky Stack

Builders stamp tools. This rough
Windows prototype lets a player

work with single blocks, a small
platform, a line, or a

three-cell run labeled stairs.
The run follows the selected

shape and direction. It does not
solve a whole staircase for you.

The exist- -ing ground still
matters. The interesting part is

where the gesture begins and
ends. Before the click, a stamp

needs a footprint you can
inspect. Every proposed cell

belongs to the preview. If one
part would leave the island,

meet an occupied cell, hit the
height limit, or cost more

material than you have, the
whole proposal must remain a

proposal. Without that boundary,
a click can leave two placed

pieces and one unexplained gap.
The player has to discover what

happened, count what was spent,
and repair a shape they never

asked to build. The source
validates the complete footprint

before spending or placement. It
also includes rollback paths for

spending and placement failures.
That is the machinery behind a

simple expectation. Either this
little thing fits, or it stays

in your hand. Open the full-size
contract sketch, authored

explanation, not a game
screenshot. Source derived

contract sketch. The blocked
example is an alternative to

successful placement, not a step
that leads to it. Three cells

illustrate the east-facing ramp
run. After the click, a

successful multi-cell stamp goes
into history as one batch. One

undo attempts to remove that
batch and refund its materials.

The source checks that every
target still has the expected

block at its top before removal.
If those checks fail, it reports

undo failed and keeps the
history entry. It does not

promise that the world can
always be wound backwards. That

limit matters. A reassuring
label should not turn a changed

world into somebody else's
cleanup job.

There are tradeoffs. A bounded
stamp is quicker to preview and

easier to understand than a
free-form blueprint editor. It

also offers fewer shapes.
Grouping the gesture makes

reversal coherent, but undoing
one piece within the group

remains a separate editing task.
Something worth trying again.

The hypothesis is that a player
will explore more freely when

the preview, material cost, and
reversal all describe the same

gesture. We have not measured
that with players here. A useful

next observation is small. Ask
someone to place a three-cell

run, reject a blocked proposal,
and undo a successful one.

Before they press undo, ask what
they expect to disappear. Watch

whether the result matches the
thing they believed they made.

The island can keep its weather,
critters, and pastel

strangeness. Underneath it, the
editor needs a dependable idea

of that thing I just did. A
little room to try, a way back

that fits the gesture. Study
Scope Slash Source Reading. A

gesture to question. This study
reads Sky Stack Builders stamp

placement and undo
implementation. The source

describes complete footprint
checks, grouped placement, and

an attempted reversal with
material refunds. The

illustrations are authored
explanations, not game captures.

No native game session or player
study was run for this note.

Source reading does not
establish every failure path or

what a player expects undo to
do. The proposed observation

remains the next study. You have
been listening to Moth and

Gravel Field Notes. The written
edition is at mothandgravel.com.
